narratives.claim: Cash/DBT schemes launched shortly before an election cause the incumbent to win
narratives.strongestCase: Bihar 2025 (Mahila Rozgar Yojana, ~6 weeks before polling, NDA's biggest win since 2010) and Madhya Pradesh 2023 (Ladli Behna, ~5 months out, BJP's best swing since 2013) both fit the pattern tightly on the numbers.
narratives.strongestCounter: Andhra Pradesh 2024 (one of India's largest state DBT programmes, YSRCP still lost by a landslide), Telangana 2023 (Rythu Bandhu unchanged, BRS still lost), West Bengal 2026 (a benefit hike ~2.5 months before polling, TMC still lost after 15 years), and Tamil Nadu 2026 (DMK's scheme running 2.5 years, DMK still lost to a brand-new party) are four elections in this same file where a fresh or freshly-hiked scheme did not save the incumbent.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A properly powered study with booth-level or survey-microdata evidence isolating the scheme's marginal effect from turnout, campaign spending, anti-incumbency and opposition quality — this file has none of that; it has election outcomes and scheme dates, which can show correlation and its absence but not a causal estimate.

narratives.claim: Madhya Pradesh 2023: Ladli Behna delivered the BJP's win
narratives.strongestCase: BJP's vote share rose 7.6 points and seat count by 54 in the one election cycle where this specific scheme existed; the scheme was the dominant theme of both the BJP campaign and post-defeat Congress commentary.
narratives.strongestCounter: MP had run other Ladli-branded schemes since 2007 without preventing a 2018 near-loss; Congress also ran a competing cash promise in 2023; the swing could equally reflect Kamal Nath's weak campaign, BJP's late leadership reset, or anti-Congress consolidation unrelated to the scheme.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: District- or booth-level correlation between Ladli Behna registration density and BJP vote-share swing, net of 2018 baseline support — not present in this file.

narratives.claim: Telangana 2023: Rythu Bandhu was not enough to save BRS
narratives.strongestCase: Rythu Bandhu ran unmodified through the election; BRS still lost 49 seats and 10 points of vote share to Congress, whose own guarantees (Mahalakshmi, farm loan waiver) plus corruption allegations against BRS and general fatigue after two terms are the more commonly cited drivers.
narratives.strongestCounter: One could argue BRS's loss would have been larger without Rythu Bandhu's base of large-farmer support — a counterfactual this file cannot test.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Comparative constituency-level analysis of BRS vote-share decline by Rythu Bandhu beneficiary density.

narratives.claim: Andhra Pradesh 2024: the largest DBT programme in the sample still lost
narratives.strongestCase: YSRCP ran Rythu Bharosa, Amma Vodi, Cheyutha and other transfers for a full five-year term, among the largest DBT welfare architectures of any Indian state in this period, and still lost 124 of 135 contested seats it had held, with vote share collapsing.
narratives.strongestCounter: Some of YSRCP's own supporters argue the loss reflects a united opposition (TDP-BJP-Janasena) and money/media asymmetry rather than welfare-policy rejection, and that welfare delivery itself was not repudiated in exit polling.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: AP-specific post-poll survey data on whether DBT beneficiaries defected from YSRCP at a materially different rate than non-beneficiaries — not in this file's source set.

narratives.claim: Karnataka 2023: Congress won by promising, not by having already delivered
narratives.strongestCase: Gruha Lakshmi and Congress's other four 'guarantees' were campaign promises made before the May 2023 poll; the schemes themselves were only launched (or in one case never fully launched — the ₹2,500 Mahalakshmi cash in neighbouring Telangana shows the same pattern) after Congress had already won and taken office. The dated record in this file settles this: launch postdates the election.
narratives.strongestCounter: None on the pure sequencing question; the open question is how much causal weight the *promise* itself carried versus other factors (BJP's Bommai-era corruption allegations, the anti-Hindutva backlash after hijab/halal controversies).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: N/A on sequencing (documented); causal weight would need survey data on when voters say they decided, and why.

narratives.claim: Delhi 2025: AAP lost despite a decade of free power/water, and BJP won while promising an even larger cash scheme
narratives.strongestCase: AAP's fresh ₹2,100/month promise, layered on top of its long-running free electricity and water subsidies, did not prevent a 26-seat collapse; BJP's competing ₹2,500/month promise (larger than AAP's) accompanied a 13-point vote-share swing in BJP's favour.
narratives.strongestCounter: The liquor-policy corruption case and ten years of incumbency fatigue are independently large factors this file cannot separate from the welfare-promise comparison; it is also possible AAP's promise was simply not believed given the party's fiscal position by that point.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Survey data on why AAP's promise did not move the seats BJP's did, isolating credibility, amount, and incumbency-fatigue effects — not in this file.

narratives.claim: West Bengal 2026: the closest-timed benefit hike in this file preceded the incumbent's defeat
narratives.strongestCase: TMC raised Lakshmir Bhandar by ₹500/month roughly 2.5 months before polling — the shortest announcement-to-poll gap of any hike in this file — and still lost after 15 years, ending its run against a BJP surge.
narratives.strongestCounter: The margin (BJP ~207 vs TMC's much smaller tally, on preliminary figures) is wide enough that most observers point to a multi-year erosion (organisational decline, corruption allegations, and a sustained BJP push since 2019) rather than treating the hike's timing as decisive either way.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: District-level correlation between Lakshmir Bhandar density and TMC vote-share retention versus decline — not in this file.

narratives.claim: Bihar 2025: the closest launch-to-poll gap in this entire file
narratives.strongestCase: First disbursement 26 September 2025, polling began 6 November 2025 — about six weeks — reaching over a crore women, ahead of the NDA's largest seat margin since 2010; opposition parties and some commentators explicitly called this an inducement.
narratives.strongestCounter: The NDA's own framing (continuation of the pre-existing Jeevika SHG programme, paced by verification, not invented for the poll) is a live, unresolved dispute this file records as a contra rather than settling; Bihar's improved law-and-order narrative and Mahagathbandhan's internal seat-sharing friction are independently cited as large factors.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Comparison of Jeevika SHG disbursement timelines in non-election years to see whether a six-week-to-poll gap is normal programme cadence or an outlier.

narratives.claim: Rajasthan's and Himachal Pradesh's welfare pushes are dwarfed by structural anti-incumbency
narratives.strongestCase: Rajasthan has changed its ruling party in every single assembly election since 1993, and Himachal Pradesh has done so in nearly every election since 1985; in this file's 2000-2026 window the combined Rajasthan+Himachal+Punjab incumbent win rate is 1 in 15, regardless of which party was in office or what it had just spent on welfare.
narratives.strongestCounter: One could argue the welfare push in each case narrowed the margin even if it did not change the outcome — a counterfactual this file cannot test with the data it has.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Margin-of-defeat trends over multiple cycles correlated with welfare spending as a share of the state budget — not in this file.

voids.what: No independent, pre-registered causal evaluation (RCT, regression discontinuity, or similar) isolating any single scheme's electoral effect from turnout, campaign spending, media coverage and opposition quality exists in this file's source set.
voids.whyItMatters: Every timing-outcome pairing in this file is a correlation over a small, non-random sample of high-profile schemes; without a causal design, both the 'cash buys votes' and the 'cash is just welfare, unrelated to the result' readings remain compatible with the same numbers.

voids.what: Booth-level or constituency-level beneficiary-density data linked to vote-share change is absent for every scheme in this file except the one Lokniti-CSDS finding cited for Maharashtra's Ladki Bahin.
voids.whyItMatters: Aggregate state-level win/loss outcomes cannot show whether beneficiaries voted differently from non-beneficiaries; the one case where such survey data exists (Maharashtra) shows a real but modest (11-point) gap, not a landslide-explaining one — the absence of equivalent data for the other 27 schemes is itself informative about how thin the public evidence base for this entire genre of claim actually is.

voids.what: This file's elections array covers 16 major states plus the Lok Sabha; it does not cover Kerala, Puducherry, the smaller northeastern states beyond Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Goa, or the Union Territories, several of which had their own election cycles and welfare schemes in this period (e.g. Kerala 2021/2026, UP 2022, Gujarat 2022).
voids.whyItMatters: The base rates in this file are drawn from a 16-state, 28-scheme sample chosen for scheme prominence and party-symmetry coverage, not from an exhaustive national census; a fuller dataset could shift the base rates, particularly the party-level ones where n is already small (e.g. AAP n=2, BRS n=1, BJD n=1).

symmetryCheck: The same question — months from scheme launch (or announcement, where launch postdated the election) to the next poll, and whether the incumbent won — was asked of every party in the sample without exception: BJP (PM-KISAN, PMGKAY, Ujjwala, MP Ladli Behna/Ladli Laxmi, Assam Orunodoi, Odisha Subhadra, Maharashtra Ladki Bahin), INC (MGNREGA, 2008 loan waiver, Chhattisgarh 2018 loan waiver, Karnataka Gruha Lakshmi, Rajasthan Mehangai Rahat, Himachal OPS), TMC (Lakshmir Bhandar, Kanyashree), DMK (Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thogai), AIADMK (Amma Unavagam), BRS (Rythu Bandhu), YSRCP (Rythu Bharosa, Amma Vodi), BJD (KALIA), JMM (Maiya Samman), AAP (Delhi free power, Delhi Mahila Samman promise, Punjab free power), and JD(U) (Mahila Rozgar Yojana). Every party in the sample has at least one case that fits the 'scheme timing helped' narrative and at least one that fits the 'scheme timing was not enough' or 'promise, not launch, mattered' narrative, with the partial exceptions of BRS, BJD, DMK, TMC and AIADMK, which in this file's window each show more counter-fitting than fitting cases (Telangana 2023, Odisha 2024, Tamil Nadu 2026, West Bengal 2026) — a pattern this file records rather than smooths over. Modi's July 2022 'revdi culture' speech against freebies is recorded as an entity/event in the PMGKAY scheme's context even though it was delivered by the same government that ran PM-KISAN, PMGKAY, Ujjwala and (via state units) MP Ladli Behna, Assam Orunodoi and Maharashtra Ladki Bahin — the same lens applied to BJP's own state and central schemes as to every opposition-run one.
gaps: MP Ladli Behna Yojana's exact announcement and launch calendar dates could not be pinned against a fetched primary source this session (Wikipedia has no standalone article; the official portal confirms the ₹1,000→1,250→1,500 amount progression but not dates); this file uses a ~5-month pre-poll estimate flagged throughout as approximate rather than asserting false day-level precision.

The BJP Delhi government's Mukhyamantri Mahila Samridhi Yojana (the ₹2,500/month promise that helped win the 2025 election) has no confirmed rollout date in this file's source set — logged rather than guessed.

Exact cabinet-approval dates (as distinct from announcement/launch dates) are missing for most state schemes in this file; where a scheme has an 'approved' object it is because a source explicitly named the approving body and date, not because approval is assumed to equal announcement.

Seat-change and vote-share figures in the elections array are only populated for the subset of rows this session specifically verified via search or fetch (2023 MP/KA/TG, 2024 AP/OR/JH/MH, 2025 Bihar/Delhi, 2026 WB/TN/AS, 2021 WB, 2022 PB); the remaining ~65 rows carry date/incumbent/winner/CM only, sourced to the standard Wikipedia article-naming convention as a pointer, per this project's stated allowance to use Wikipedia as a pointer to primary sources — not as a claim that every number for those rows has been independently checked.

This file's elections array covers 16 states plus the Lok Sabha, not all 28 states/8 UTs; Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Puducherry and several northeastern states beyond Assam are out of scope for this pass (see voids).

Beneficiary counts and outlay figures are left null for schemes where this session did not find a session-verified figure (e.g. PM-KISAN, PMGKAY, MGNREGA, MP Ladli Behna, AP Rythu Bharosa/Amma Vodi, WB Lakshmir Bhandar/Kanyashree, TN Kalaignar/Amma Canteen, Assam Orunodoi's later phases, Maharashtra Ladki Bahin's precise outlay) rather than estimated from memory.

No independent academic or CAG evaluation of targeting accuracy, leakage or ghost beneficiaries was located for 27 of the 28 schemes in this file (see voids) — this is a gap in available oversight literature, not a finding that those schemes are clean.

The Lok Sabha 2004-2019 rows' precise CM/PM swearing-in dates and the pre-2018 state election seat/vote-share numbers rely on general, well-established public knowledge rather than a session-specific fetch; where this matters for a scheme's own electionContext (i.e. the marquee cases), a session-verified source is cited directly on the scheme record instead.

This file's WebSearch budget was a shared, session-level allocation across a concurrent research fleet and was exhausted partway through this task; remaining verification (particularly Punjab's pre-2017 seat/vote-share detail, and Jharkhand's 2005-2014 coalition CM sequencing) relied on WebFetch and general knowledge rather than further search.

Party-level base rates in this file have very small n per party (AAP n=2, BRS n=1, BJD n=1, DMK n=1, AIADMK n=1, TMC n=2) and should not be read as characterising a party's general behaviour — they describe this file's specific 28-scheme sample only.
